children.value: A retrieval system rarely shows the raw output of a vector search to its users. In

, embeddings served as a first stage: a bi-encoder retrieves a few hundred candidates, and a cross-encoder reorders them with a stronger and more expensive model. Media retrieval follows the same pattern. A compact color feature finds candidate images, and a more detailed comparison puts them in their final order. For such a first stage, the exact nearest neighbor has no special value. What matters is that the good matches are among the candidates, because the second stage decides their order.

Even without a second stage, users want to see good matches, not necessarily the single best one. The previous section showed that high dimensions reduce contrast: the nearest neighbor is only marginally closer than the next few points, and all of them stand out clearly from the background. Returning the third-best match instead of the best one hardly changes what the user sees. This opens the door to a trade: we give up exactness and gain speed.

How can we accelerate the search? A full scan reads every vector, so its cost is the number of vectors times the size of each vector. A concrete collection makes this tangible. One billion embeddings with 768 dimensions, stored as 4-byte floats, occupy

children.html: 109×768×410^9 \times 768 \times 4109×768×4

children.value: bytes, about 3 TB. A full scan reads all 3 TB for every query. There are three levers to reduce this volume, and this section treats them in turn:
: map the vectors into a lower-dimensional space.
: store each vector as a compact code.
: visit only the part of the collection near the query.
Each lever trades a little accuracy for speed. Combined, they reduce the work per query by two to three orders of magnitude.
The first lever shrinks every vector before the search starts.
(PCA) finds the directions along which the data varies most and projects every vector onto the leading ones. It works well when the original dimensions are not independent. The color histogram of

is a good case. Neighboring bins cover similar intensities, so a slightly brighter photograph moves pixels from one bin into the next. Correlated dimensions carry overlapping information, and a few principal components capture most of it. Distances in the reduced space then approximate the distances in the original space well.
Embeddings can be trained for this purpose. The Matryoshka embeddings of

arrange their information so that the leading dimensions carry the most significant part, and a prefix of the vector is itself a usable embedding. Truncation needs no projection at all, only a shorter read.

Dimensionality reduction is a modest lever. Depending on the features, it removes roughly 20 to 60 percent of the data without changing the results much. Reducing our example collection from 768 to 384 dimensions halves 3 TB to 1.5 TB. Every vector must still be read, so the search remains a full scan, only a cheaper one.

The second lever keeps the dimensions but stores each vector with fewer bits. A float uses 32 bits per component, far more precision than a similarity comparison needs. The errors that compression introduces are small compared to the gap between good matches and the background, so they rarely change which matches stand out.
The simplest form replaces each float with a small integer. We divide the value range of each dimension into

children.value: intervals and store only the number of the interval that contains the value. With

Quantization does not have to give up exactness. The

(VA-file) of Weber, Schek, and Blott (1998) accepts the conclusion of the previous section: if every leaf must be read anyway, make reading cheaper. The interval numbers of a vector describe a cell of a grid, and from the cell we can compute a lower and an upper bound on the distance between the query and any vector inside it. The search first scans the compact approximations and discards every vector whose lower bound exceeds the

Skipping the exact comparisons turns the same codes into an approximate method. Scalar quantization is therefore the bridge between exact and approximate search.

The second lever gains between a factor of 4 for 8-bit scalar quantization and roughly a factor of 100 for short LSH codes, with product quantization typically in between at 16 to 64. Every vector is still read, but each one costs only a fraction of a full comparison.
The third lever reduces the number of vectors read. This was the idea behind the tree structures in

: skip regions that cannot contain the answer. The previous section showed that exact pruning fails in high dimensions, because the sphere around the query intersects every region. Approximate methods relax the requirement. They visit only the regions most likely to contain good matches and accept that a neighbor just across a boundary may be missed.

A different approach navigates a graph. A

(NSW) graph turns every vector into a node and links it to a fixed number of its nearest neighbors, its “friends”, plus some long-range links that act as shortcuts across the space. The graph has two key properties. It is
: from any node, a step to the neighbor closest to the query makes progress toward the query. And it is a
: any two nodes are connected by a short path, whose length grows only poly-logarithmically with the number of nodes.
Search starts at an entry point and greedily moves to whichever neighbor is closest to the query, as traced in

. It stops when no neighbor is closer than the current node. This node is a local minimum of the distance on the graph, not necessarily the global one, which is why the result is approximate. To reduce the risk of stopping early, the search keeps a list of the best

children.value: candidates instead of a single node and expands all of them. A longer list costs more steps and finds better neighbors.

children.value: version, HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016), stacks several such graphs. The base layer contains all vectors. Each higher layer contains a random subset of the layer below, with fewer and fewer nodes toward the top. It then descends layer by layer, using the best node of each layer as the entry point for the next one, and refines the result on the base layer. Two parameters control the index:

No single lever wins on its own, so production libraries combine all three. Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) is the standard example. It organizes an index into four stages, which map directly onto the levers:
prepare vectors: PCA to reduce dimensions (lever 1), or L2-normalization for cosine search.
select the vectors to read, for example with IVF or HNSW (lever 3).
encode the selected vectors compactly, for example with scalar quantization, PQ, or LSH (lever 2).

The plot quantifies the trade. The full scan reaches 16.5 queries per second at a recall of 1.0. The fastest method at each recall level does far better:

Approximation buys two to three orders of magnitude, and the last few points of recall are the most expensive. The plot does not show everything, though. Memory use and build time appear in separate plots on the benchmark site, and they are where methods differ most: HNSW needs its graph and the full vectors in memory, while PQ needs a fraction of the memory and builds quickly.

The ann-benchmarks view makes approximation look costly. The last points of recall are expensive, and many cheap configurations return only a third of the exact top 10. But recall against exact search compares one retriever with another. A user never sees the exact top 10. The user sees the final result of a pipeline, and its quality is measured against relevance judgments with nDCG, as in

We test this on TREC-COVID: 171,332 abstracts of COVID-19 research papers, 50 topics, and graded relevance judgments. The retrievers combine the three levers. Matryoshka embeddings from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B are truncated to between 1024 and 64 dimensions. A full scan, IVF, or HNSW selects the vectors, and exact floats, PQ codes, or LSH bits compare them. This gives 140 retrievers. Each returns its top 50, and the cross-encoder Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B reorders them into the final top 10. TREC judged only the documents that the systems of 2020 retrieved, so the pool from

misses documents that only an approximate retriever surfaces. An LLM judge graded these missing pairs. Otherwise they would count as not relevant and penalize exactly the retrievers we want to evaluate.

measures every retriever in three ways. We focus on the 126 retrievers that read at least 100 times less data than a full scan. Against exact search (left), their median recall@10 is 0.24, so the typical cheap retriever returns only a quarter of the exact top 10. By this measure, approximate search fails. Judged for relevance (middle), the same top 10 reach a median nDCG@10 of 0.80, against 0.91 for exact search. The documents they return instead of the exact neighbors are often just as relevant. This is the loss of contrast from

at work: the exact neighbors are only marginally nearer than the next candidates, and many of those candidates are good matches too. After reranking (right), the median rises to 0.88, against 0.92 for exact search, and 44 percent of the cheap retrievers end within 0.03 of exact search.

follows five retrievers through the pipeline. One retriever uses 256 dimensions, 16 of 1,024 IVF lists, and 32-byte PQ codes. It reads 608 times less data than a full scan and returns only a third of the exact top 10, yet after reranking it reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.92, the same as exact search. HNSW on 64-dimensional embeddings reads 2,604 times less data with the same result. Once a reranker follows, even aggressive Matryoshka truncation costs almost nothing.

The two remaining retrievers show where this stops. PQ with 8 bytes per vector distorts the distances so strongly that only 6 percent of the exact top 10 survive, and on its own it reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.66. Many relevant documents are still among its 50 candidates, so the reranker lifts the result to 0.80 and repairs more than half of the gap. IVF with a single probed list fails differently. It never reads the clusters next to the query’s own cluster, so the reranker never sees their documents, and the result stays at 0.86 before and after reranking.
Fine-filter errors are repairable; coarse-filter errors are not.
Production systems therefore keep the coarse filter generous, with enough probed lists or a long candidate list, and let the fine filter be aggressive.

There is no single best method, only the best operating point for a given collection, memory budget, and quality target. Recall against exact search is a useful diagnostic for one index, but the operating point should be chosen on end-to-end quality: the cheapest retriever whose reranked result stays close to that of exact search. The benchmark above covers one collection and one embedding model, so the operating point must be measured again for each application. HNSW is a strong default as long as the vectors fit into main memory. Beyond that, IVF with product quantization and a final reranking step is the common choice.
